newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW - China's CITIC wants Australian food.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW - China's CITIC wants Australian food.

text.p: After doubling its export sales over the past two years, the Australian food and agricultural produce arm of China's biggest capitalist-style enterprise is at the beginning of what it feels is a steeply-rising growth path.
CITIC Australia Food Pty Ltd, part of China International Trust and Investment Corp (CITIC), is little more than two years old but its positioning in Australia is already paying off.
Modernising Asia increasingly wants imported food. CITIC is a natural channel for imports into China. And Australia is the foodbowl of the Asia-Pacific region.
All three groups show a focus on agricultural exports as a main new growth area. "Everything is growth," Hamilton said.

While Korea's Samsung Co Ltd group has been making spectacular investment forays into Australian pastoral land, in January 1994 CITIC became Australia's second-largest meat processor by acquiring Adelaide-based Metro Meat.
This put CITIC behind only U.S.-owned ConAgra Inc's Australian Meat Holdings in Australia's meat processing industry, ahead of Nippon Meat Packers Inc of Japan.
CITIC's component in the sale was only 45,000 tonnes, part of Australia's total of 180,000 tonnes.
But after three years of smaller containerised grain export deals, the Pakistan deal was CITIC Australia's first bulk sale.
"Yes, it's a breakthrough," Hamilton said.
Now CITIC Australia is chasing other Australian bulk grains contracts, confident it has added a new business dimension.
The first Asian trading houses to enter Australia in pursuit of the commodities trade were Japanese, then came the South Koreans, now they are joined by China, through CITIC.

CITIC Australia as a whole has built its investment in Australia from nil in 1986 to more than A$500 million. CITIC Australia Foods holds about A$25 million of total group investments, excluding Metro Meat.
"There is potential for that to grow. China is huge and growing," Hamilton said.

Like most Asian traders, CITIC likes the long-term view, with wheat a classical example. CITIC Australia Food was positioning itself in the Australian grain market in anticipation of de-regulation in Australia and China, he said.
Hamilton said Metro Meat, which contributes about 20 percent of CITIC Australia Food's sales, faces strong Asian demand for a wide range of products and by-products.
Some demand is for specialised products for the Asian taste, other for prime meat cuts, as Asian taste swings West.

CITIC would invest further in Australian meat if it saw a business which fitted well. But it does not plan to follow Samsung into major pastoral investments, preferring to use contract growers for both meat and wheat production.
CITIC's ability to move into private grains trading would greatly increase if the Australian Wheat Board de-regulated, losing its monopoly on wheat exports, he said.
Of Japanese, Korean and Chinese trading houses in Australia -- "it's in the blood," Hamilton said.
That instinct has established a partial monopoly for CITIC on Australian agricultural exports to China, with much of its exports distributed by CITIC central command in Beijing.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
